note: Legal routes are conditional entitlements, not guarantees: eligibility depends on facts not supplied (source of funds, ID classification, tax records). Prohibited routes carry risk information only and deliberately contain no execution steps.

methods.name: Documented current-account income wire (foreign individual)
methods.who: 境外个人 (foreign individual per S01 Art. 37: a non-PRC-ID holder, e.g. a U.S. citizen without a mainland resident ID) with lawful RMB income earned in China (salary, services, royalties, rent, etc.).
methods.rule: S01 Art. 13: a foreign individual's lawful current-account RMB income may be purchased into FX and remitted with ID and transaction-amount evidence, including tax documents. S02 Art. 13(1) repeats the tax-document requirement. No annual USD total is stated for this route in either text; the bank reviews authenticity.
methods.docs: Passport/ID; employment or service contract; income evidence; Chinese tax payment voucher (税务凭证); remittance application; receiving-account details.
pros: No published per-year USD ceiling in the rule text (unlike the domestic-individual quota).
Tax already paid on the income means the conversion itself adds no Chinese tax (S09 Art. 2 — conversion is not a taxable category).
One documented route can move the whole balance in one or several wires.
cons: Requires a genuine documented income trail with tax vouchers; undocumented savings do not qualify.
Bank has authenticity-review discretion; processing may take longer for large amounts.
Wire fees and FX margin apply at every transfer (see ladder L1).
steps: Confirm with the bank that the account holder is classified as 境外个人 (foreign individual) under S01 Art. 37, and that the balance has a current-account income trail.
Assemble documents: passport, employment/service contract, income statements, Chinese individual-income-tax payment vouchers for the amounts involved.

At the bank (counter or eligible e-banking channel), submit a FX purchase (购汇) application for the CNY amount with the supporting documents; bank records it through the SAFE personal FX system (S02 Art. 6, 32–36).
Submit the outward remittance (汇出) application to the destination account you own; pay the published handling fee and cable fee (S06).
Keep the exchange slip (兑换水单) and remittance receipt; they support §988 basis records and re-conversion rights (S02 Art. 13(2)).

Reconcile U.S. reporting for the year: worldwide income (S13), FBAR if foreign accounts exceeded USD 10,000 aggregate (S10), Form 8938 if thresholds met (S11), and §988 gain if the CNY appreciated since receipt (S14).

methods.name: Annual USD 50,000 convenience quota (domestic individual)
methods.who: 境内个人 (domestic individual per S01 Art. 37: PRC citizen holding a mainland resident ID). A U.S. citizen who also holds a PRC resident ID may fall here; classification is a bank determination (flag F01).
methods.rule: S02 Art. 2: settlement and FX purchase are managed under an annual total of USD 50,000 equivalent per person per year; within the total, ID only is required (S01 Art. 9).
methods.docs: Valid ID. (Above-quota amounts need transaction evidence — see M03.)
pros: Simplest lawful channel: ID only, no income documents within the quota.
Cumulative quota across banks is tracked through the SAFE personal FX system (S02 Art. 32–36).
cons: Hard ceiling of USD 50,000 per calendar year per person — USD 400,000 needs 8 years (or more persons, which is prohibited structuring if organized to evade limits — see P01).
Uses of purchased FX cannot include overseas property, securities or insurance (S08).
Each wire carries its own fee and cable charge (ladder L2 shows chunked costs).
steps: Verify remaining quota for the calendar year with the bank (personal FX settlement system).
Purchase USD within the remaining annual total with ID; conversion at the bank's published sell rate (S07 board is a reference snapshot only).
Remit to the overseas account you own; ≤ USD 50,000/day cumulative from an FX savings account is handled on ID alone (S02 Art. 14).
Repeat in later calendar years for larger balances; keep every exchange slip and remittance receipt.
File U.S. reporting as in M01 step 6.

methods.name: Above-quota documented current-account purchase and remittance (domestic individual)
methods.who: 境内个人 with current-account income (salary, services, royalties, family support, inheritance receipts, insurance payouts, investment income) beyond the annual total.
methods.rule: S02 Art. 10 lists the evidence per income type (employment: contract + income proof); Art. 12 covers above-quota purchases with transaction-amount proof; S01 Art. 12 covers above-quota outbound remittance with authenticity documents.
methods.docs: ID plus the Art. 10 evidence for the income type (e.g. employment contract + income proof + tax records), and transaction-amount proof for the purchase.
pros: Removes the USD 50,000 ceiling for genuine documented current-account income.
Same bank-wire mechanics and published tariff as the quota route.
cons: Document assembly is heavier; banks scrutinize large amounts.
Chinese income tax compliance on the underlying income is expected; unpaid-tax situations are not cured by paperwork.
steps: Classify the balance by true income type per S02 Art. 10 and collect the matching evidence (contracts, income proof, tax payment records).
Submit above-quota FX purchase at the bank with ID + evidence; bank records the transaction in the personal FX system.
Remit abroad with authenticity documents; cash remittance over USD 10,000/day needs extra slips per S02 Art. 14 (bank-account remittance ≤ USD 50,000/day by ID, above with proof).
Keep all slips; complete U.S. reporting for the year (S10, S11, S13, S14).

methods.name: Mainland property sale proceeds repatriation
methods.who: 境外个人 (non-resident) who sold a self-owned mainland commodity house; S01 Art. 22 permits FX purchase and remittance of the RMB proceeds with SAFE-approval framework; S05 gives the operational steps sourced from Bank of China.
methods.rule: S01 Art. 22; S05 steps; S03 Section VI simplified related approvals. The sale itself is a taxable event in China (asset-transfer income, S09 Art. 2(8)/Art. 3(3) flat 20% on income — actual computation and any local concessions not verified, blank in tables).
methods.docs: Passport; commodity-house transfer contract and registration certificate; tax-payment voucher from the local tax authority; Tax Filing Form for External Payments when the transaction exceeds USD 50,000; notarized power of attorney if an agent acts.
pros: Explicitly lawful channel with a published step list.
S03 Section VI removed mandatory staged remittance and document notarization requirements.
cons: Chinese tax on the sale must be settled first and evidenced (S05 steps 3–4).
Tax amount depends on facts (holding period, cost basis, local practice) — left blank (flag F05).
Bank and SAFE review of paperwork; timelines vary.
steps: Complete the sale: property-ownership review, contract signing, ownership transfer registration (S05 steps 1–2).
Settle the property-sale tax at the local tax authority and obtain the tax-payment proof (S05 step 3).
Obtain the Tax Filing Form for External Payments for Trade in Services and Other Accounts from the tax authority if the amount exceeds USD 50,000 (S05 step 4).
At the bank, purchase FX with the proceeds and remit, presenting passport, contract, registration certificate, tax voucher and (if applicable) the filing form and power of attorney (S05 step 5).

Retain all receipts; report U.S. side: FBAR/8938 for the account, and any U.S. tax effects of the sale (S10, S11). Property-sale gain taxation on the U.S. side depends on facts and is blank (flag F01/F06).

methods.name: Emigration property transfer (移民财产转移)
methods.who: A person who emigrated abroad (or settled in HK/Macau) and held lawful mainland property before obtaining emigrant status — the 2004 Measures frame it for Chinese emigrants; a U.S. citizen in this project may or may not qualify (flag F01).
methods.rule: S02 Art. 20 routes emigration transfers to the 2004 Interim Measures (S04); S03 Section VI simplified approvals: approval at former household registration SAFE office, HQ filing for totals over RMB 500,000 removed, mandatory staged remittance removed (approved amount may go out once or in parts), property-rights document notarization dropped.
methods.docs: Identity + emigration-status documents (e.g. household-registration cancellation proof per S04); property-rights evidence; lawful-source evidence; SAFE approval document; bank remittance papers.
pros: Designed for exactly this use: converting pre-emigration assets and sending them abroad.
2014 reforms made it faster (no forced batches, no HQ filing, no notarization).
cons: Requires formal SAFE approval; property must be lawful, undisputed and free of judicial restriction (S04).
2004 text on staged remittance (Art. 6) conflicts with S03 Section VI — implementation varies by office (flag F09).
Approval and document work are slow; professional help is often needed (cost unverifiable — blank).
steps: Determine eligibility under S04: the property must pre-date emigrant status and be lawful, undisputed, unrestricted.
Apply to the SAFE branch at the former household registration place (S03 Section VI(1); S04 Art. 5) with identity, emigration and property documents.
Receive the SAFE approval document specifying the approved amount.
At the bank, purchase FX and remit within the approved amount, once or in several remittances (S03 Section VI(2)).
Retain approval, slips and receipts; complete U.S. reporting (S10, S11).

methods.name: Inheritance property transfer (继承财产转移)
methods.who: Foreign citizens (or HK/Macau residents) who lawfully inherit mainland estate (S04). U.S. heirs of mainland property fit here; also relevant to the reverse case flagged in F01.
methods.rule: S02 Art. 20; S04 defines the route; S03 Section VI(3)-(4): inheritors from several decedents may consolidate applications at one office; notarization of property-rights documents removed.
methods.docs: Inheritance legal documents or notarized instruments (S02 Art. 10(3)); identity; property evidence; SAFE approval; bank papers.
pros: Lawful capital route for heirs with a genuine estate.
Consolidated application allowed across decedents (2014 reform).
cons: SAFE approval required; estate must be lawful and undisputed.
Estate tax and income-tax treatment in China and the U.S. depends on facts (blank; flag F05/F01).
Cross-border estate administration is document-heavy.
steps: Obtain inheritance legal documents (court judgment, notarized succession certificate, etc. per S02 Art. 10(3)).
Apply to the SAFE branch at the decedent's last household registration place (S03 Section VI(1); S04 Art. 5).
After approval, sell/liquidate assets if needed, settle any Chinese taxes, purchase FX and remit once or in parts (S03 Section VI(2)-(3)).

Keep the full paper trail; U.S. reporting may include FBAR/8938 and possibly Form 3520 for foreign gifts/bequests — Form 3520 requirement cited in prior editions is IRS-published but not re-fetched in this edition (flag F16).

methods.name: Personal foreign-trade settlement account (个人对外贸易经营者)
methods.who: An individual who completed business registration and foreign-trade operator filing (S02 Art. 9(1)).
methods.rule: S01 Art. 10; S02 Art. 9: trade FX receipts and settlement run through the individual's FX settlement account and are managed like institutional accounts — no annual total limit (SAFE press Q&A for S02 confirms settlement accounts are not subject to the annual total).
methods.docs: Business registration / trade-operator filing; trade contracts; customs declarations or, for agency exports, agency contracts + logistics documents (S02 Art. 9(2) as amended by Huifa [2016] No. 13); invoices.
pros: No annual quota ceiling for genuine trade flows.
Suited to actual exporters/importers with trade documents.
cons: Only for real trade — using it to relabel savings is false-documenting (P03).
Institutional-account bank pricing is not the personal e-banking tariff; modeled costs are flagged (F13).
Requires ongoing compliance (registration, declarations, verification).
steps: Register the business and file for foreign-trade operator status (S02 Art. 9(1)).
Open the personal FX settlement account at a designated bank (S02 Art. 25).
Receive export proceeds into the settlement account with trade documents; settle (结汇) per institutional rules without the annual total.
Purchase FX for genuine import payments or remit per trade terms; keep customs declarations and contracts.
Complete international-payments declarations (S01 Art. 8) and U.S. reporting for the accounts and income.

methods.name: Family support, gifts and other documented inbound transfers
methods.who: Domestic individuals receiving family support (赡家款), notarized gifts, or similar one-way current-account transfers from abroad (S02 Art. 10(1)-(2)).
methods.rule: S02 Art. 10: above-quota settlement of gifts requires a notarized gift agreement; family support requires kinship proof + donor income evidence (bank proof, tax payment certificate). The money then follows quota or above-quota purchase rules (M02/M03).
methods.docs: Notarized gift agreement or kinship proof; donor's income evidence (bank deposit certificate, personal income tax voucher); IDs of both parties.
pros: Lawful for genuine family flows.
Can supplement the annual quota with documented above-quota settlement.
cons: Genuine family relationship and donor income must be evidenced.
Gifts must comply with national rules (S02 Art. 10(1)).
Not a device to move the user's own savings — that is structuring (P01).
steps: Have the donor send the transfer with a clear purpose and retain donor income evidence.
Settle at the bank within the annual total on ID; above it, present notarized gift/kinship documents (S02 Art. 10).
Purchase FX and remit per M02/M03 rules as applicable.
Keep records on both sides; U.S. persons receiving foreign gifts may have Form 3520 duties (flag F16).

methods.name: Wise from-CNY transfer (licensed-provider route)
methods.who: Non-mainland-Chinese individuals (Taiwan/HK/Macau eligible) who worked in China and hold a China tax record showing tax paid within the last 3 years; personal accounts only; recipient must be an account the sender owns (S17).
methods.rule: Provider terms under a PBOC-regulated licensed third-party payment partner (S17). Limits: CNY 300,000 per transfer via China bank app, CNY 50,000 via Alipay; overall limit derived from after-tax salary proven by tax records; limits do not expire.
methods.docs: Wise verification (1–2 working days first time); China tax records within the last 3 years; Chinese bank account or Alipay; destination account the sender owns.
pros: Digital onboarding; no counter visit.
Overall limit tied to documented after-tax salary — can exceed the bank quota route for eligible earners.
Funds arrive in an account you own abroad.
cons: Eligibility excludes mainland-Chinese senders and anyone without recent China tax records.
No fixed published fee table — exact fees appear only at transfer setup (S17); all fee cells blank (F07).
Single-transfer caps force multiple transfers at larger amounts.
steps: Check eligibility: non-mainland-Chinese sender with China work/tax history (S17).
Complete Wise verification once (1–2 working days) and upload qualifying tax records to set the overall limit.
Create the transfer to your own overseas account; pay from the China bank app (≤ CNY 300,000) or Alipay (≤ CNY 50,000).
Compare Wise's live quote against the bank quote for the same net USD before sending; Wise's fee is only knowable at quote time (F07).
Keep records; complete U.S. reporting (S10, S11).

methods.name: Bank-card overseas spending with post-return FX repayment
methods.who: Anyone with a mainland-issued bank card spending or withdrawing abroad within card rules; the FX-purchase repayment after return does not count toward the annual total (S08; S02 Art. 35(5)).
methods.rule: S08: 个人境外旅游消费刷卡支付的，回国后购汇还款不计入年度总额 — overseas card spending repaid by FX purchase after return is outside the annual-quota system; S02 Art. 35(5) keeps such repayments outside the personal FX settlement system.
methods.docs: Card and statement; repayment via the card account.
pros: Does not consume the USD 50,000 quota for the repayment leg.
No wire fee or wire paperwork per transaction.
Lawful for genuine consumption/withdrawal needs.
cons: This spends money abroad; it does not deliver cash to a U.S. bank account.
Card issuer FX conversion, ATM and withdrawal fees are not verified from official schedules here (blank; flag F08).
Card networks enforce their own overseas withdrawal caps (not verified here).
steps: Use the mainland-issued card for genuine overseas purchases or ATM withdrawals.
Repay the card in CNY after returning; the FX-purchase repayment stays outside the annual total (S08).
Keep statements; there is no transfer receipt since no wire occurs.
For large future conversions, this is a consumption channel, not a repatriation channel.

methods.name: Physical cash carrying with declaration and permits
methods.who: Any traveler crossing the border with FX cash.
methods.rule: S19/S20: outbound ≤ USD 5,000 equivalent no permit; USD 5,000–10,000 with bank-issued FX Carrying Permit; over USD 10,000 requires SAFE permit (and per S20 is tied to travel to specified countries); inbound over USD 5,000 must be declared; RMB limit CNY 20,000 per crossing.
methods.docs: Customs declaration form; bank or SAFE issued 携带证 (FX Carrying Permit) when applicable; ID.
pros: No wire or correspondent fees.
Simple for small amounts within the permit-free band.
cons: Strict hard caps; over-limit cash without permits is returned or confiscated with fines (S19).
Insurance, security and travel costs are unpriced here (blank).
USD 400,000 cannot lawfully cross at once; many trips would look like evasion and are impractical.
Cash still needs lawful-source answers on both sides of the border.
steps: Convert CNY to USD cash at the bank within applicable purchase rules (M02/M03 for the purchase leg).
For USD 5,000–10,000, obtain the bank-issued FX Carrying Permit before departure (S19/S20).
Declare cash at customs per the thresholds; keep the declaration form.
Deposit in the destination bank; expect source-of-funds questions for large cash deposits (U.S. banks file currency transaction reports — not fetched here; blank F14).

methods.name: Company profit/dividend remittance from a foreign-invested enterprise
methods.who: A foreign individual/shareholder receiving genuine declared profits from a company they invested in (FIE route; S03 Section V).
methods.rule: S03 Section V: banks handle profit remittance ≤ USD 50,000 equivalent without document review; above, board/partner profit-distribution resolution + original tax-filing form required, with the bank stamping the form after remittance.
methods.docs: Board/partner profit-distribution resolution; tax-filing form (tax authority); company audit basis for distributable profit; shareholder identity.
pros: Explicitly facilitated channel for genuine distributions (2014 reform).
Above USD 50,000 the document list is short and fixed.
cons: Requires a real profitable company with declared dividends; it cannot relabel personal savings.
Corporate tax and dividend withholding precede remittance (rates not modeled — blank F05).
Company bank pricing differs from the personal tariff (F13).
steps: Declare dividends via the company with a board/partner resolution; settle corporate-level taxes per Chinese tax rules.
Obtain the tax authority's tax-filing form for external payments.
Have the bank remit the profit (≤ USD 50,000 simplified; above, present resolution + original tax-filing form — S03 Section V).
Bank stamps the tax form with the actual remitted amount and date; keep copies.
U.S. side: dividend income reporting and foreign tax credit (Form 1116, S15); FBAR/8938 for accounts (S10, S11).

methods.name: Insurance payout settlement (foreign-exchange insurance proceeds)
methods.who: Domestic individuals receiving FX insurance payouts under compliant policies (S02 Art. 10(4), 19).
methods.rule: S02 Art. 10(4): above-quota settlement with insurance contract + insurer payment proof; Art. 19: payouts may be held in the FX savings account or settled to RMB. FX life-insurance premiums themselves are restricted (Art. 19; S08 bars using FX purchase for life/investment insurance abroad).
methods.docs: Insurance policy; insurer payment certificate; ID.
pros: Documented route for genuine claims/payouts.
Payout can stay in FX without settlement.
cons: Only for lawful policies; only payout amounts qualify.
Niche: not a route for general savings.
steps: Receive the payout into the FX savings account with policy and payment proof (S02 Art. 19).
Settle or remit per quota/above-quota rules (M02/M03).
Keep policy, payout proof and slips; complete U.S. reporting.

methods.name: Unused-RMB re-conversion on original exchange slip (foreign individual)
methods.who: 境外个人 who converted FX to RMB earlier and has not used it all (S01 Art. 15; S02 Art. 13(2)).
methods.rule: S02 Art. 13(2): unused converted RMB may be converted back to FX on the original exchange slip, valid 24 months from conversion; daily small amounts (≤ USD 500, or ≤ USD 1,000 pre-departure in restricted zones) need ID only. S01 Art. 14: unspent FX originally remitted in can be returned by the original route with ID.
methods.docs: Original exchange slip (兑换水单); ID; for larger amounts the slip is mandatory.
pros: Restores FX without income documents — it is a reversal, not a new purchase.
Original-route refund of remitted-in FX is even simpler (S01 Art. 14).
cons: Only covers amounts traceable to a slip within 24 months — not general savings.
Then the FX still needs a lawful remittance leg to leave China.
steps: Locate the original exchange slip(s) within the 24-month validity (S02 Art. 13(2)).
At the bank, convert the unused RMB back to USD against the slip.
Remit the FX abroad (S02 Art. 15 for foreign individuals: by ID from FX savings account).
Keep the new slip; report as usual.

methods.name: Qualified domestic institutional overseas investment (QDII-type)
methods.who: 境内个人 investing abroad through qualified domestic institutions (banks, fund managers) per S01 Art. 17 / S02 Art. 17.
methods.rule: S01 Art. 17 / S02 Art. 17: domestic individuals may use FX or RMB for overseas fixed-income and equity investment through qualified domestic institutional investors; employee stock plans go through the employer/agent with SAFE approval (S02 Art. 18).
methods.docs: Product subscription documents at the qualified institution; KYC.
pros: Lawful capital-account outflow channel for investment purposes.
Institution handles FX and remittance mechanics.
cons: Money ends up invested, not in a U.S. bank account; redemption is a separate step.
Product fees/prices are not verified here (blank).
S08 confirms FX purchase may not be used for overseas securities directly — this route works only through the qualified institutions framework.
steps: Choose a qualified domestic institution product (S02 Art. 17).
Subscribe with RMB or FX; institution performs the conversion and outbound investment formalities.
Hold/ redeem per product terms; proceeds follow the product's return rules.
Report foreign accounts/securities on FBAR/8938 as applicable (S10, S11).

methods.name: Structuring: splitting transfers or using relatives' quotas
methods.rule: S01 Art. 7 forbids splitting (分拆) to evade limit supervision; S08 forbids lending one's quota or borrowing others' (不得出借本人或借用他人额度). Banks detect patterns through the personal FX system (S02 Art. 32–36).
cons: Explicitly prohibited; transactions can be rejected, accounts restricted, and penalties applied.
Pattern detection is systematic, not anecdotal.
No execution steps are provided by design.

methods.name: Underground banking (地下钱庄) / black-market exchange
methods.rule: S08 explicitly names underground-banking participation as a violation; PBOC/SAFE enforcement treats such value transfer as illegal; associated money-laundering crimes are prosecuted (context in S18's list of harms).
cons: Criminal exposure (illegal business operations, money laundering) plus total-loss risk on funds.
No recourse if the counterparty disappears.
No execution steps are provided by design.

methods.name: False trade documents, over-invoicing or sham services
methods.rule: S01 Art. 7 forbids using false commercial documents or vouchers to evade authenticity management; S08 forbids false declarations and untrue materials.
cons: Customs/tax/AML cross-checks compare invoices, logistics and payments.
Criminal fraud and tax-evasion exposure on top of FX penalties.
No execution steps are provided by design.

methods.name: Cryptocurrency / stablecoin cash-out
methods.rule: S18 (Yin Fa [2021] No. 237): fiat-crypto exchange and related services are illegal financial activities, strictly banned; offshore exchanges serving domestic residents are likewise illegal; virtual currency has no legal-tender status.
cons: Declared illegal financial activity in China; counterparties and platforms are enforcement targets.
Funds can be frozen during investigations; contract protections do not apply.
U.S. tax treatment of crypto dispositions is separate and adds reporting complexity (not a tax-free channel).
No execution steps are provided by design.

methods.name: Misusing FX purchase quota for overseas property, securities or insurance
methods.rule: S08: 个人购付汇不得用于境外购房、证券投资、购买人寿保险和投资性返还分红类保险 — FX purchase/remittance may not be used for overseas home purchase, securities investment, life insurance or investment-linked insurance. (Investment abroad goes only through qualified institutions — M15.)
cons: Banks ask purchase purpose and can require evidence; false purpose is the fraud route P03.
Transactions can be reversed and quota privileges suspended.
No execution steps are provided by design.

methods.name: Letting others move money through your account (money-mule / pass-through)
methods.rule: S01 Art. 36 requires banks to record, analyze and report large or suspicious FX transactions under AML rules; S08 forbids money laundering participation.
cons: AML monitoring flags third-party flows; account freezes are common.
Criminal accessory exposure for laundering or illegal FX operations.
No execution steps are provided by design.
